name: Negativity bias
statement: Negative information is said to weigh more than positive information of the same size, a principle usually summarised as bad is stronger than good.
meaning: Three claims travel under one name and rest on different literatures. The first is about weighting: negative information counts for more than positive information when someone forms an impression. The second is about duration: bad events leave affective consequences that outlast good ones of matching size. The third is about the body: negative material draws a larger physiological response. Rozin and Royzman cut the idea a fourth way, into negative potency, steeper negative gradients, negativity dominance and negative differentiation. Negativity dominance is their sharpest version, and their abstract defines it as combinations of negative and positive entities yielding evaluations more negative than the algebraic sum of the individual valences would predict. Support for any one of these is routinely reported as support for all of them.

origin.who: Roy F. Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer and Kathleen D. Vohs
origin.note: "Bad Is Stronger Than Good" ran to 48 pages and gathered findings from everyday events, trauma, close relationships, social networks and learning. Crossref dates it to December 2001 and dates Rozin and Royzman's taxonomy in Personality and Social Psychology Review to November 2001, a month earlier, and Baumeister and colleagues cite it on their first page as in press. Neither paper coined the phenomenon; both were attempts to give a scattered literature one name.

evidence: Both founding statements are reviews rather than meta-analyses, and Baumeister and colleagues set their own method apart from both. They write that "Unlike more focused narrative reviews or meta-analyses, we were unable to conduct a systematic search using keywords such as good or bad". A request to the Society for Personality and Social Psychology list-serve drew roughly 100 responses, and those responses were the starting point for the search. They also state their priority plainly: "The consistency of conclusions across each area is more important than the robustness or methodological strength of evidence in each specific area." Their abstract concludes that hardly any exceptions, meaning findings of greater power of good, can be found. The string "effect size" appears nowhere in the 48 pages, and the review reports no pooled estimate. Rozin and Royzman's abstract describes a review of literary, historical, religious and cultural sources alongside the psychological literatures on learning, attention, impression formation, contagion, moral judgement, development and memory; their full text could not be obtained here. Brannon and Gawronski open their 2018 paper by citing Pratto and John's automatic-vigilance work as their example of the attention finding and Kanouse and Hanson as their example of the impression-formation one.

replication.headline: A registered report on 12,448 randomised headline trials found negative words raise clicks, while a preregistered replication of the cross-national physiological result missed significance.
replication.detail: The strongest test is a registered report whose stage 1 protocol was accepted in principle on 11 March 2022. Robertson, Pröllochs, Schwarzenegger, Pärnamets, Van Bavel and Feuerriegel analysed the confirmatory half of the Upworthy Research Archive. That archive holds 22,743 randomised trials in which rival headlines for the same story were served to real readers between 24 January 2013 and 14 April 2015, drawing about 5.7 million clicks across more than 370 million impressions. Those two totals belong to the whole archive. Preregistered filtering left 12,448 trials and 53,699 headlines, which took 2,778,124 clicks across over 205 million impressions, and 53,699 is the observation count the regression table reports. The figure captions give 53,669 for the same quantity, and no reconciliation appears in the article text. A larger proportion of negative words raised the odds of a click, beta = 0.015, SE = 0.001, z = 17.423, 99% CI [0.013, 0.018]. For a headline of average length, 14.965 words, each negative word lifted the click-through rate by 2.3 percent. Each positive word cut it by about 1.0 percent, beta = -0.008, SE = 0.001, z = -9.238, 99% CI [-0.010, -0.006]. Two preregistered emotion predictions failed. Fear was predicted to raise clicks and lowered them, beta = -0.007, z = -5.919, and an equivalence test on anger was undecided, p = 0.399, 99% CI [-0.003, 0.002]. The physiological claim holds on average and comes apart at the level of the person. Soroka, Fournier and Nir ran one protocol on 1,156 respondents in 17 countries across six continents, recording heart-rate variability and skin conductance while people watched real video news. Shifting story tone from positive to negative moved heart-rate variability by 10 percent of its observed standard deviation, and skin conductance measured 20 seconds into a story by 65 percent. Taken country by country, the mean coefficient cleared zero on a one-tailed t test in 5 of 17 countries for heart-rate variability and 9 of 17 for skin conductance. In New Zealand and Sweden the skin-conductance effect ran the other way, though not reliably. Country explains 1.5 percent of the variance in individual coefficients for heart-rate variability and 2.7 percent for skin conductance, so the spread sits between people rather than between cultures. Dubèl, Schumacher, Homan, Peterson and Bakker ran a preregistered replication of the skin-conductance result in the Netherlands, recruiting 104 and analysing 97. Their negativity coefficient ran in the predicted direction and missed the preregistered threshold, beta = 0.019, t = 0.984, p = 0.325, against 0.042 in the original. They write that their study "failed to replicate the statistical significance of the effect reported by SFN". Their added measure of negative affect, activity in the corrugator muscle, was itself marginal on the preregistered model, beta = 0.038, t = 1.926, p = 0.054. It reached significance only on a simplified model they did not preregister, beta = 0.060, p < 0.001. Their participants rated positive clips as more arousing than negative ones, M = 6.45 against M = 4.76, t = -8.28. The impression-formation literature has been split apart rather than overturned. Brannon and Gawronski ran three experiments, 1,058 people beginning and 972 analysed, on whether new negative information violates an expectancy more than new positive information does. It did not, at either amount of prior information, and they conclude that the bias arises when people reconcile an inconsistency rather than when they notice one. Sperlich and Unkelbach found no negativity bias in evaluative conditioning across five preregistered experiments, 394 in the laboratory and 391 online. It appeared once they made one valence rare. Rare negative outcomes produced a negativity bias, and rare positive outcomes produced a positivity bias. Paolini, Gibbs, Sales, Anderson and McIntyre meta-analysed valenced intergroup contact across 238 independent samples, 936 nested effects and 152,985 people, and report that the harm from negative contact is significantly larger than the benefit from positive contact. On duration, Luhmann, Hofmann, Eid and Lucas pooled 313 samples and 65,911 people from 188 publications, across marriage, divorce, bereavement, childbirth, unemployment, reemployment, retirement and relocation. They report that the effects of life events on wellbeing "are not a function of the alleged desirability of events", which cuts against ranking events by how bad they were.

study.cite: Robertson, C. E., Pröllochs, N., Schwarzenegger, K., Pärnamets, P., Van Bavel, J. J., & Feuerriegel, S. (2023). Negativity drives online news consumption. Nature Human Behaviour, 7(5), 812-822.

limits: The verdict covers the general principle rather than any one of its parts, and the parts do not move together. Negative language raising news consumption is preregistered and it held. Greater physiological response to negative news held on average across 17 countries, did not reach conventional levels in most of them taken singly, and missed significance in a preregistered Dutch replication of it. Negative information dominating the identification of inconsistency did not appear in a 972-participant study designed to find it, and its authors say that result leaves the wider principle standing. Searches of Crossref and Europe PMC on 17 August 2026 turned up no Many Labs or multi-laboratory replication of the negativity bias itself; the preregistered field evidence tests headline clicks, not the laboratory paradigms the 2001 reviews were built from. Banerjee and Urminsky report no average effect of negative tone across more than 150,000 randomised headline tests on 398 news platforms and five experiments with 8,369 people. They put the direction down to whether a reader is seeking credibility or enjoyment. Their paper is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. The idea also carries weight in political science. Hibbing, Smith and Alford argued in a Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article that negativity is one organising element behind the liberal-conservative divide, with conservatives registering greater physiological responses to negative stimuli and devoting more psychological resources to them. The study behind that claim is Oxley and colleagues' 2008 report in Science, whose abstract gives 46 adults with strong political beliefs. Bakker, Schumacher, Gothreau and Arceneaux ran a preregistered direct replication with 202 participants, plus conceptual replications with 352 in the United States and 81 in the Netherlands. Their analyses did not support the original conclusions, and they found no evidence for the broader claims about disgust or about a physiological trait. Corns argues the principle should be rejected as ill-formed. Baumeister and colleagues gloss strength as causal impact and then specify it several ways at once. Corns shows those specifications are dissociable and lists more than a dozen further senses of strength drawn from their own text. His conclusion is that the results offered as evidence "could just as well be interpreted as disconfirmation as confirmation". Unkelbach, Alves and Koch offer a rival account in which positive information is more similar than negative information, so valence asymmetries follow from the structure of the environment with no processing bias behind them. Freyer and colleagues formalise both positions and conclude that a theory must say what counts as good and what counts as bad before a test of it can be informative. The intercept version of the same asymmetry has its own entry, positivity offset, no. 308.
misreadings: The 2001 papers are cited as though they were meta-analyses. They are not, and Baumeister and colleagues describe their own search as unsystematic and their emphasis as breadth rather than methodological strength. The second error is treating negativity bias as one effect with one effect size. Attention, impression formation, affective duration and physiological arousal are separate claims, and the evidence for them now points in different directions. The third is reading the cross-national result as a universal. Soroka, Fournier and Nir report an average negativity bias and also report that most of their 17 country samples would not show one alone, and their own conclusion is that this gives reason to reconsider the journalistic maxim that if it bleeds, it leads. The fourth is quoting Brannon and Gawronski's null as a defeat for the negativity bias in impression formation. Their paradigm measures whether people notice an inconsistency, and they argue the bias sits at the later stage where people resolve one. The fifth is treating negativity dominance as established because negative news gets clicked. Robertson and colleagues measured a behaviour and write that "readers' preference for headlines containing negative words does not imply that users felt more negatively while reading said headlines".
